title: General Surgery Diploma — Cell Injury and Death, Lecture 2

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: What is universally recognized as the most common cause of cell injury in clinical medicine and surgery?
options: Ionizing radiation
Hypoxia and Ischemia (loss of oxygen or blood supply)
Vitamin deficiency
Viral infection
questions.explanation: Ischemia simultaneously deprives tissues of oxygen and essential nutrients while blocking metabolic waste removal.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 2 — Causes of cell injury: • Hypoxia / Ischemia: Most common cause; loss of O2 or blood supply.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: What is the earliest ultrastructural and light microscopic manifestation of Reversible Cell Injury?
options: Pyknosis and karyorrhexis
Cellular (hydropic) swelling due to Na+/K+ ATPase pump failure
Lysosomal membrane rupture and autodigestion
Formation of myelin figures
questions.explanation: Failure of ATP-dependent Na+/K+ pumps allows intracellular sodium and water accumulation, resulting in acute cellular swelling ('cloudy swelling').
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 4 & Slide 7 — Reversible Injury: • Cellular (hydropic) swelling | Earliest manifestation of injury; due to Na+/K+ pump failure.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: Which of the following cellular changes is considered the 'point of no return' indicating Irreversible Injury?
options: Detachment of ribosomal units from the endoplasmic reticulum
Mild mitochondrial swelling with small amorphous densities
Severe mitochondrial damage with failure of ATP generation and extensive plasma membrane damage
Mild chromatin clumping in the nucleus
questions.explanation: Profound mitochondrial dysfunction and structural plasma membrane breakdown mark the irreversible threshold leading to cell death.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 4 — Irreversible Injury: • Irreversible Injury: Severe mitochondrial damage: ATP production fails | Extensive plasma membrane damage | 'Point of no return' - leads to necrosis or apoptosis.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: What are the five primary biochemical mechanisms of cell injury discussed in the lecture?
options: ATP Depletion, Mitochondrial Damage, Influx of Calcium, Oxidative Stress (ROS), and Membrane Damage
Hypertrophy, Atrophy, Metaplasia, Hyperplasia, and Dysplasia
Pyknosis, Karyorrhexis, Karyolysis, Apoptosis, and Necrosis
Steatosis, Lipofuscin, Hemosiderin, Melanin, and Glycogen
questions.explanation: These five interconnected pathways represent the core biochemical routes through which lethal stimuli destroy cellular homeostasis.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 5 — Mechanisms of cell Injury: • MECHANISMS: ATP Depletion | Mitochondrial Damage | Calcium Influx | Oxidative Stress / ROS | Membrane Damage.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: How does severe intracellular ATP depletion directly cause cellular swelling?
options: By activating caspase-8
By failing the Na+/K+ ATPase pump, causing net influx of sodium and water into the cell
By increasing glycogen synthesis
By dissolving nuclear chromatin
questions.explanation: Without ATP, active sodium extrusion stops, osmotically drawing water into the intracellular compartment.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 16 — Mechanism 1 (ATP Depletion): • Failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump -> Na+ and water enter the cell -> cellular swelling.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: What metabolic consequence occurs when cells shift to anaerobic glycolysis due to oxygen deprivation and ATP depletion?
options: Intracellular accumulation of lactic acid, causing intracellular pH to fall
Increased oxidative phosphorylation
Elevation of intracellular pH (alkalosis)
Accelerated protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Anaerobic glycolysis rapidly consumes glycogen stores and accumulates lactic acid, dropping intracellular pH and denaturing enzymes.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 16 — Mechanism 1 (ATP Depletion): • Compensatory anaerobic glycolysis increases -> lactic acid accumulates -> intracellular pH falls.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: What triggers the opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) during cell injury?
options: Sustained cytosolic calcium influx, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and oxygen deprivation
High intracellular potassium levels
Excessive ATP production
Normal physiological growth factors
questions.explanation: mPTP opening collapses the mitochondrial membrane potential, halting oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 11 — Mechanism 2 (Mitochondrial Damage): • Triggered by rising cytosolic Ca2+, reactive oxygen species, and oxygen deprivation itself -> Opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore -> mitochondria fail to make ATP.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: Which pro-apoptotic mitochondrial protein leaks into the cytosol when mitochondria are damaged, triggering the intrinsic apoptotic cascade?
options: Albumin
Cytochrome c
Hemoglobin
Fibrinogen
questions.explanation: Cytosol accumulation of cytochrome c binds Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, activating caspase-9.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 11 — Mechanism 2 (Mitochondrial Damage): • Leakage of cytochrome c into the cytosol activates the intrinsic apoptotic pathway.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: What are the downstream pathological consequences of a sustained massive influx of calcium into the cytosol?
options: Activation of destructive enzymes: phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, and ATPases
Enhanced ATP synthesis and cell proliferation
Stabilization of plasma membranes
Upregulation of glycogen storage
questions.explanation: Elevated cytosolic calcium turns on destructive degradative enzymes that dismantle cellular structures.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 13 — Mechanism 3 (Loss of Calcium Homeostasis): • Sustained high Ca2+ activates damaging enzymes: Phospholipases (degrade membranes), Proteases (break down cytoskeleton), Endonucleases (fragment DNA), ATPases (hasten ATP depletion).

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: How do Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) cause structural damage to cells?
options: By lipid peroxidation of membranes, protein cross-linking/fragmentation, and DNA strand breaks
By stimulating active mitosis
By repairing damaged mitochondria
By increasing intracellular pH
questions.explanation: Free radicals with unpaired electrons aggressively steal electrons from lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 13 — Mechanism 4 (Oxidative Stress): • Damage Targets: Lipid peroxidation of membranes | Protein cross-linking & fragmentation | DNA strand breaks.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: Which cellular membrane systems are damaged during severe cell injury, and what are their specific consequences?
options: Plasma membrane (fluid/ion influx), Mitochondrial membrane (ATP collapse/cytochrome c leak), and Lysosomal membrane (hydrolytic enzyme autodigestion)
Nuclear membrane only (no other membranes affected)
Endoplasmic reticulum only (ribosomes multiply)
Golgi apparatus only
questions.explanation: Lysosomal rupture releases acid hydrolases into the cytoplasm, digesting all cellular macromolecules (autodigestion).
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 7 & Slide 19 — Mechanism 5 (Membrane Damage): • Plasma membrane damage: influx of fluid and ions | Mitochondrial membrane damage: ATP collapses, cytochrome c leaks | Lysosomal membrane damage: hydrolytic enzymes leak out -> autodigestion.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: What is Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury, and in which surgical scenarios is it particularly critical?
options: Injury sustained during cold storage only; irrelevant to surgery

Tissue injury that paradoxically intensifies when blood supply is restored to ischemic tissue, driven by a ROS burst and neutrophil influx; critical in organ transplantation, vascular clamp release, cardiopulmonary bypass, and tourniquet use
Injury caused exclusively by bacterial superinfection
Chronic venous stasis ulceration
questions.explanation: Reperfusion introduces molecular oxygen to compromised cells, sparking an oxidative burst, complement activation, and massive neutrophil-mediated injury.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 3 — Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury: • Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury: blood supply return to tissue after period of ischemia -> ROS burst & inflammation | Relevant to: organ transplantation, vascular clamp release, cardiopulmonary bypass, tourniquet use.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: What macroscopic appearance does an organ exhibit during early Reversible Cellular (Hydropic) Swelling ('cloudy swelling')?
options: Dark red, shrunken, and firm
Pallor, increased turgor, and increased organ weight
Transparent and gelatinous
Completely liquefied and pus-filled
questions.explanation: Distension of cells and intracellular organelles by water increases organ bulk and creates a pale, turbid gross appearance.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 7 — Cellular (Hydropic) Swelling: • Grossly: pallor, increased turgor, and increased organ weight ('cloudy swelling').

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: What is Fatty Change (Steatosis), and in which organ is it most frequently observed?
options: Accumulation of triglyceride lipid vacuoles within the cytoplasm, especially in the liver
Deposition of calcium in heart valves
Accumulation of glycogen in the brain
Fibrous scarring of skeletal muscle
questions.explanation: Disruption of lipid metabolic pathways by toxins (alcohol), hypoxia, or metabolic disorders causes intracellular triglyceride droplet accumulation.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 7 & Slide 23 — Fatty Change (Steatosis): • Fatty Change (Steatosis): Hypoxic, toxic, or metabolic injury - especially in the liver | Lipid vacuoles accumulate within the cytoplasm.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: According to the ultrastructural comparison table, how do mitochondria appear in Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury?
options: Reversible: Normal; Irreversible: Completely absent
Reversible: Swelling with few small densities; Irreversible: Marked swelling with large amorphous densities
Reversible: Ruptured; Irreversible: Intact
Reversible: Dense and shrunken; Irreversible: Hyperactive
questions.explanation: Appearance of dense flocculent densities within swollen mitochondrial matrices signifies point-of-no-return irreversible damage.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 8 — Ultrastructural Comparison Table: • Mitochondria: Reversible = Swelling, few small densities | Irreversible = Marked swelling, large amorphous densities.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: What ultrastructural nuclear changes mark Irreversible Cell Injury (Necrosis) in chronological order?
options: Hypertrophy → Hyperplasia → Metaplasia → Dysplasia
Pyknosis (nuclear shrinkage/condensation) → Karyorrhexis (nuclear fragmentation) → Karyolysis (chromatin fading/dissolution)
Mitosis → Meiosis → Apoptosis → Regeneration
Vacuolization → Blebbing → Swelling
questions.explanation: Sequential enzymatic breakdown and shrinkage of the nucleus define the classic nuclear hallmarks of necrotic cell death.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 6 — Sequence of Nuclear Change: • 1. Pyknosis (Nucleus shrinks, chromatin condenses) -> 2. Karyorrhexis (Nucleus fragments) -> 3. Karyolysis (Chromatin fades, DNase digestion).

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: What is the key difference in endoplasmic reticulum and lysosome integrity between Reversible and Irreversible Injury?
options: Reversible: ER dilation & ribosome detachment, lysosomes intact; Irreversible: ER extensive disruption with myelin figures, lysosomes ruptured releasing enzymes
Reversible: Lysosomes ruptured; Irreversible: Lysosomes intact
Reversible: Myelin figures present; Irreversible: ER completely normal
There is no structural difference
questions.explanation: Lysosomal rupture and accumulation of whorled phospholipid masses ('myelin figures') distinguish irreversible necrosis.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 8 — Ultrastructural Comparison Table: • Endoplasmic reticulum: Reversible = Dilation; ribosome detachment | Irreversible = Extensive disruption; myelin figures | Lysosomes: Reversible = Intact | Irreversible = Ruptured, enzymes released.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: Which of the following describes the fundamental biological nature of Necrosis?
options: Regulated, energy-dependent programmed cell death without inflammation
Uncontrolled, energy-independent cell death occurring in living tissue that triggers an inflammatory response and is always pathologic
Physiological cell turnover during embryogenesis
Reversible adaptation to stress
questions.explanation: Necrosis represents accidental cell destruction, spilling intracellular contents and inciting acute inflammation.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 6 — Necrosis General Features: • Necrosis: Uncontrolled, energy-independent cell death occurring in living tissue. Triggers an inflammatory response and is always pathologic.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the six major morphologic patterns of necrosis?
options: Coagulative Necrosis
Liquefactive Necrosis
Proliferative Necrosis
Caseous Necrosis
questions.explanation: Proliferative necrosis is a distractor; the six recognized patterns are coagulative, liquefactive, caseous, fat, fibrinoid, and gangrenous.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 2 — Lecture Overview & Slide 6–22: • Necrosis Patterns: Coagulative, Liquefactive, Caseous, Fat, Fibrinoid, Gangrenous.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.topic: Causes, Mechanisms & Reversible vs. Irreversible Injury
questions.stem: What is the cellular hallmark of Reversible Injury that allows full recovery if the stimulus is removed?
options: Resolution of cellular swelling, restoration of ATP production, and intact membranes
Complete dissolution of nuclear DNA
Permanent replacement by fibrous scar tissue
Formation of apoptotic bodies
questions.explanation: If injury is mild or brief, reversal of ionic and metabolic derangements restores normal cell structure and function.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 4 & Slide 5 — Reversible Injury: • Resolves fully if the injurious stimulus is removed | Cellular swelling, mild mitochondrial swelling, dilation of ER, membrane blebbing.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is the characteristic histological and gross pattern of Coagulative Necrosis?
options: Complete enzymatic liquefaction into pus
Denaturation of structural proteins and enzymes preserves basic tissue architecture (ghost outlines of cells), classic for ischemic death in solid organs like heart, kidney, and spleen
Cheese-like friable white appearance caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Saponification of fat by calcium
questions.explanation: In coagulative necrosis, cellular outlines remain faintly visible ('ghost cells') for days due to coagulated structural proteins inhibiting lytic enzymes.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 6 — Coagulative Necrosis: • Coagulative Necrosis: Denaturation of structural proteins and enzymes preserves the basic tissue architecture | Classic pattern of hypoxic death in solid organs: heart, kidney, liver, spleen.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Why does hypoxia in the Central Nervous System (CNS/brain) result in Liquefactive Necrosis rather than Coagulative Necrosis?
options: Because brain tissue lacks blood vessels
Because brain tissue has high lipid content, scant stroma, and abundant hydrolytic enzymes that rapidly digest dead neural tissue into a viscous liquid mass
Because the brain undergoes caseous necrosis
Because neurons have rigid cell walls
questions.explanation: Unlike solid organs where structural proteins coagulate, CNS tissue lacks structural collagen/stroma and liquefies completely upon cell death.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 17 — Liquefactive Necrosis: • Liquefactive Necrosis: Dead cells are completely digested by hydrolytic enzymes, leaving a liquefied, viscous mass | Typical pattern of hypoxic death in central nervous system (high lipid content, scant stroma).

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Which clinical condition is the classic example of Coagulative Necrosis resulting from ischemia?
options: Acute Myocardial Infarction (heart attack)
Brain abscess
Pulmonary tuberculosis granuloma
Acute pancreatitis
questions.explanation: Coronary artery occlusion cuts off oxygen, producing classic coagulative necrosis in the myocardial wall.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 6 — Coagulative Necrosis Example: • Classic example: Myocardial infarction.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What are the classic clinical settings for Liquefactive Necrosis?
options: Focal bacterial or fungal infections (abscess/pus formation) and brain infarcts
Atherosclerotic peripheral vascular disease
Caseous granulomas in the lung
Pancreatic fat saponification
questions.explanation: Leukocyte recruitment during acute infection releases powerful lysosomal enzymes that liquefy tissue into pus.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 17 — Liquefactive Necrosis Settings: • Characteristic of focal bacterial or fungal infections (enzymes from recruited leukocytes drive digestion) and hypoxic death in CNS.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is Caseous Necrosis, and which infectious organism is its classic hallmark?
options: Liquefaction of brain tissue caused by staphylococcus
Friable, white, 'cheese-like' appearance in the center of granulomas caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Fibrinoid deposition in blood vessels caused by hypertension
Saponification of fat caused by pancreatic enzymes
questions.explanation: 'Caseous' (cheesy) necrosis features acellular, granular eosinophilic debris surrounded by epithelioid macrophages and Langhans giant cells.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 26 — Caseous Necrosis: • Caseous Necrosis: Complete destruction of tissue architecture caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis | Grossly: friable, white, 'cheese-like' appearance at center of granulomas.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What histological and gross features characterize Fat Necrosis?
options: Destruction of adipose tissue by lipases or trauma, liberating free fatty acids that combine with calcium to form chalky white deposits ('saponification')
Liquefaction of the brain into pus
Caseous white granulomas in the lung
Fibrinoid ring formation around arterioles
questions.explanation: Released pancreatic lipases break down fat cell triglycerides; liberated fatty acids bind calcium to form insoluble chalky white soap deposits.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 24 — Fat Necrosis: • Fat Necrosis: Destruction of adipose tissue due to action of lipases or trauma | Free fatty acids combine with calcium 'saponification' -> chalky white deposits grossly | Classic example: Acute pancreatitis, breast fat necrosis.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Which two surgical conditions are classic examples of Fat Necrosis?
options: Acute pancreatitis and breast trauma (breast fat necrosis)
Appendicitis and cholecystitis
Inguinal hernia and varicocele
Hemorrhoids and anal fissure
questions.explanation: Pancreatic duct disruption releases active enzymes into peripancreatic fat, while blunt breast trauma causes localized fat necrosis mimicking carcinoma.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 24 — Fat Necrosis Examples: • Classic example: Acute pancreatitis, breast fat necrosis.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is Fibrinoid Necrosis, and in which conditions is it classically identified?
options: Necrosis of bone in osteomyelitis

Deposition of immune complexes and leaked plasma proteins/fibrin within blood vessel walls, producing a bright pink, amorphous appearance on H&E; seen in Polyarteritis nodosa and malignant hypertension
Liquefaction of skeletal muscle
Caseous necrosis of lymph nodes
questions.explanation: Type III hypersensitivity reactions or severe hypertension damage vessel walls, leaking plasma proteins and fibrin ('fibrinoid').
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 20 — Fibrinoid Necrosis: • Fibrinoid Necrosis: Deposition of immune complexes, fibrin and plasma proteins within the wall of blood vessels | Bright pink, amorphous appearance | Identifies underlying immune-mediated vasculitic process (Polyarteritis nodosa, malignant hypertension).

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What defines Gangrenous Necrosis in a surgical context?
options: A distinct primary pattern of cell death caused directly by viruses
Clinical term for ischemic death of tissue (typically involving a lower limb or bowel) complicated by secondary bacterial infection and putrefaction
Programmed cell death during embryogenesis
Benign degeneration of adipose tissue
questions.explanation: Gangrene is not a unique cell death mechanism per se, but rather ischemic coagulative necrosis (often involving multiple tissue planes) modified by bacterial superinfection.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 22 — Gangrenous Necrosis Surgical Relevance: • Gangrenous Necrosis: Death of tissue caused by loss of blood supply, often complicated by secondary bacterial infection and putrefaction.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What are the key clinical and pathological differences between Dry Gangrene and Wet Gangrene?
options: Dry: Caused by ischemia alone without significant infection, mummified, dry, black with a clear line of demarcation; Wet: Ischemia with bacterial superinfection, foul-smelling, swollen, lacking a clear line of demarcation (surgical emergency)
Dry: Caused by bacterial infection; Wet: Caused by ischemia alone
Dry: Requires emergency amputation; Wet: Resolves with antibiotics alone
There is no difference
questions.explanation: Wet gangrene carries a high risk of lethal systemic sepsis due to active bacterial proliferation in devitalized tissue, demanding urgent debridement.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 22 — Dry vs. Wet Gangrene: • Dry Gangrene: Ischemia alone, no significant infection, mummified dry black appearance, clear line of demarcation | Wet Gangrene: Ischemia + bacterial superinfection, foul-smelling, swollen, no clear line of demarcation (surgical emergency).

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is Gas Gangrene, and what is its primary causative organism?
options: Infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus producing endotoxins
Rapidly progressive, life-threatening soft tissue infection caused by Clostridium perfringens producing gas (H2, CO2) and severe muscle necrosis
Fungal infection of the lung caused by Aspergillus
Viral infection of the liver
questions.explanation: Clostridial spores contaminate deep wounds or crush injuries; anaerobic fermentation produces tissue gas bubbles (crepitus) and profound myonecrosis.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 21 — Gas Gangrene: • Gas Gangrene: Rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection of muscle and soft tissue caused by Clostridium perfringens | Bacterial fermentation produces gas (H2, CO2), dark non-contractile muscle.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Why is Gas Gangrene considered a true surgical emergency where antibiotics alone are inadequate?
options: Because antibiotics cannot penetrate blood vessels, and necrotic tissue packed with bacteria and gas requires urgent, aggressive surgical debridement or amputation to prevent rapid mortality
Because gas gangrene resolves spontaneously within 24 hours
Because antibiotics neutralize bacterial gas bubbles instantly
Because surgery is strictly contraindicated in clostridial infections
questions.explanation: Systemic toxins and anaerobic gas dissection spread rapidly along muscle fascial planes; surgical excision of devitalized tissue is life-saving.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 21 — Gas Gangrene Clinical Pearl: • Clinical pearl: Gas gangrene is true surgical emergency — mortality rises rapidly if treatment delayed; urgent surgical removal of all dead tissue is mandatory; antibiotic alone is inadequate.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is the surgical significance of recognizing necrosis patterns during wound debridement?
options: It helps the surgeon distinguish viable from necrotic tissue at the wound margins, guiding the exact extent of surgical resection
It determines the patient's blood type
It replaces the need for anesthesia
It predicts the patient's insurance coverage
questions.explanation: Leaving necrotic, devitalized tissue at surgical margins invites wound infection and dehiscence.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 18 — Why This Matters in Surgical Practice: • Wound Debridement: Distinguishing viable from necrotic tissue at the margin's guides extent of resection.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: How does the distinction between dry and wet gangrene guide surgical management?
options: Dry gangrene can sometimes be managed expectantly or allowed to auto-amputate, whereas wet gangrene demands urgent surgical debridement or amputation due to high sepsis risk
Both conditions can always be treated with warm saline soaks
Wet gangrene never requires surgery
Dry gangrene requires immediate emergency amputation within 10 minutes
questions.explanation: Dry ischemic mummification without infection stabilizes safely, whereas wet gangrene propagates bacterial toxins and invasive sepsis.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 22 — Gangrenous Necrosis Clinical Pearl: • Clinical pearl: Wet gangrene carries a high risk of sepsis and demands urgent surgical intervention unlike dry gangrene, which can sometimes be managed expectantly.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What role does pathology play in organ transplantation regarding cell injury and death?
options: Allograft rejection involves both apoptotic and necrotic cell death pathways, and evaluating biopsy specimens guides immunosuppressive management
Transplants never experience cell injury
Pathology is only used for billing purposes
Rejection is diagnosed exclusively by blood pressure
questions.explanation: Endothelial and parenchymal cell death patterns in graft biopsies indicate acute cellular or antibody-mediated rejection.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 18 — Transplant Rejection: • Transplant Rejection: Allograft rejection involves both apoptotic and necrotic cell death pathways.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is the significance of the 'extent and pattern of necrosis' on histopathology reports for tumors or infarctions?
options: It directly correlates with clinical prognosis, tumor grade, and tissue viability
It has no clinical relevance
It only indicates the operating room temperature
It measures the patient's height
questions.explanation: Extensive tumor necrosis (e.g., in glioblastoma, renal cell carcinoma, or sarcomas) signifies aggressive biological behavior and poorer prognosis.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 18 — Prognostication: • Prognostication: Extent and pattern of necrosis on histology correlates with clinical outcome.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: In which organ is coagulative necrosis characteristically NOT seen during ischemia?
options: Heart (myocardium)
Kidney
Brain
Spleen
questions.explanation: While heart, kidney, and spleen undergo coagulative necrosis upon infarction, the brain undergoes liquefactive necrosis.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 6 & Slide 17 — Coagulative vs Liquefactive: • Notably does not occur in the brain, which undergoes liquefactive necrosis instead.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What causes the 'chalky white' appearance of fat necrosis grossly in acute pancreatitis?
options: Calcium soap formation (saponification) where liberated free fatty acids bind calcium
Fibrin deposition
Pus accumulation
Melanin pigment
questions.explanation: Precipitation of insoluble calcium soaps creates macroscopic chalky white plaques across peritoneal fat.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 24 — Fat Necrosis: • Free fatty acids combine with calcium 'saponification' -> chalky white deposits grossly.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Which form of necrosis features granulomatous inflammation with Langhans giant cells and epithelioid macrophages?
options: Coagulative necrosis
Caseous necrosis
Liquefactive necrosis
Fibrinoid necrosis
questions.explanation: Tuberculous granulomas wall off caseous necrotic debris using specialized immune cells.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 26 — Caseous Necrosis: • Caseous Necrosis: Surrounded by granulomatous inflammation with rim of epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells, lymphocytes and plasma cells.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What type of necrosis is classically associated with Polyarteritis nodosa (vasculitis)?
options: Fibrinoid necrosis
Fat necrosis
Caseous necrosis
Coagulative necrosis
questions.explanation: Immune complex deposition in arterial walls leads to vessel destruction characterized by bright pink fibrinoid necrosis.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 20 — Fibrinoid Necrosis: • Classic example: Polyarteritis nodosa; malignant hypertension.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What distinguishes the microscopic appearance of coagulative necrosis?
options: Complete cellular dissolution into fluid
Preservation of basic tissue architecture (ghost outlines of cells) with loss of nuclei
Infiltration by dense neutrophils and pus
Accumulation of myelin figures
questions.explanation: Denatured structural proteins prevent immediate enzymatic digestion, maintaining tissue architecture while nuclei undergo karyolysis/pyknosis.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 6 — Coagulative Necrosis: • Microscopically: ghost outlines of cells - cell shape preserved, nucleus lost.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What distinguishes microscopic findings in an abscess (liquefactive necrosis)?
options: Ghost outlines of cells without neutrophils
Amorphous debris, abundant neutrophils, and complete loss of cellular outlines
Caseous granulomas with giant cells
Fibrinoid vessel wall thickening
questions.explanation: Suppurative inflammation recruits vast numbers of neutrophils whose released enzymes digest tissue into purulent liquid.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 17 — Liquefactive Necrosis: • Microscopically: amorphous debris, abundant neutrophils, cellular outlines lost.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Which pattern of necrosis is specifically produced by Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
options: Caseous necrosis
Coagulative necrosis
Fat necrosis
Liquefactive necrosis
questions.explanation: Mycobacterial cell wall lipids induce hypersensitivity and characteristic caseous cheese-like destruction.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 26 — Caseous Necrosis: • Characterized by complete destruction of tissue architecture caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is the primary pathological mechanism driving fat necrosis in acute pancreatitis?
options: Activated pancreatic lipases leaking into the peritoneum and pancreatic substance
Bacterial fermentation producing hydrogen gas
Immune complex deposition in vessels
Ischemic coagulative necrosis of myocardial fibers
questions.explanation: Extravasation of active digestive enzymes autodigests peripancreatic adipose tissue.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 24 — Fat Necrosis: • Activated pancreatic lipases leak into the peritoneum and pancreatic substance, liberating fatty acids.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Which gangrene subtype requires immediate emergency surgical intervention due to high mortality from septic shock?
options: Dry gangrene
Wet gangrene and Gas gangrene
Chronic ischemic rest pain
Simple hydropic swelling
questions.explanation: Active bacterial proliferation in devitalized wet or gas gangrene rapidly seeds bacteria and toxins into the systemic circulation.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 21 & Slide 22 — Surgical Emergencies: • Wet gangrene carries a high risk of sepsis and demands urgent surgical intervention | Gas gangrene is true surgical emergency — mortality rises rapidly if treatment delayed.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What defines Apoptosis as a form of cell death?
options: Uncontrolled, energy-independent destruction with severe inflammation
A regulated, energy-dependent (ATP-requiring) programmed cell death pathway that eliminates unwanted or damaged cells without provoking inflammation
Accidental cell bursting caused by bacterial toxins
Swelling and rupture of plasma membranes
questions.explanation: Apoptosis utilizes an active enzymatic cascade to neatly dismantle cells into membrane-bound bodies engulfed by macrophages.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 9 — Apoptosis: • Apoptosis: A regulated, energy-dependent pathway that eliminates unwanted or damaged cells without provoking an inflammatory response.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Which of the following represents a PHYSIOLOGICAL role of apoptosis?
options: Viral infection killing cells via cytotoxic T-lymphocytes
Embryogenesis, hormone-dependent tissue involution, and immune cell turnover/selection
Myocardial infarction coagulative necrosis
Caseous necrosis in tuberculosis
questions.explanation: Programmed cell death sculpts tissues during development (e.g., finger web regression) and maintains homeostasis.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 9 — Apoptosis Physiologic Roles: • Physiologic Roles: Embryogenesis | Hormone-dependent tissue involution | Immune cell turnover & selection.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What are the two principal signaling pathways of Apoptosis?
options: Coagulative and Liquefactive pathways
Intrinsic (Mitochondrial) Pathway and Extrinsic (Death Receptor) Pathway
Aerobic and Anaerobic pathways
Dystrophic and Metastatic pathways
questions.explanation: Both pathways converge on the activation of executioner caspases that systematically dismantle the cell.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 12 — Apoptosis Pathways: • Two Pathways, One Execution Program: Intrinsic (Mitochondrial) Pathway | Extrinsic (Death Receptor) Pathway.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What triggers the INTRINSIC (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis?
options: Internal cellular stress such as irreparable DNA damage, growth factor withdrawal, or severe cell stress
Binding of external Fas ligand to cell surface death receptors
Bacterial lipopolysaccharide endotoxin
High extracellular sodium concentration
questions.explanation: Sensor proteins detect internal damage, neutralizing protective Bcl-2 proteins and permeabilizing mitochondrial membranes.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 12 — Intrinsic Pathway: • Intrinsic (Mitochondrial) Pathway: Triggered by internal stress such as growth factor withdrawal or DNA damage | Regulated by Bcl-2 family proteins -> mitochondrial membrane permeabilization.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What triggers the EXTRINSIC (death receptor) pathway of apoptosis?
options: Internal mitochondrial cytochrome c release
External signaling molecules binding to cell surface death receptors (e.g., Fas receptors / TNF receptor family)
Intracellular calcium overload
Lactic acid accumulation
questions.explanation: Ligand binding (e.g., FasL) clusters cell surface death receptors, recruiting adaptor proteins and activating initiator caspase-8.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 12 — Extrinsic Pathway: • Extrinsic (Death Receptor) Pathway: Triggered by external signals binding to death receptors (Fas receptors) -> Caspase-8 activation.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Which enzymes act as the primary executioners of apoptosis once activated by intrinsic or extrinsic cascades?
options: Lipases and Amylases
Caspases (proteolytic enzymes that degrade cellular proteins and DNA)
Histones and Albumins
ATPases and Phosphatases
questions.explanation: Caspases cleave structural cytoskeletal proteins and nuclear lamins, orchestrating neat apoptotic fragmentation.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 12 — Caspases: • Caspases are proteolytic enzymes act as main executioner of apoptosis, once activated, they degrade cellular proteins and DNA, leading to orderly cell death.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What are the key microscopic and macroscopic morphological features of Apoptosis?
options: Cell swelling, membrane disruption, and massive acute inflammation
Cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, membrane blebbing, formation of apoptotic bodies, and phagocytosis by macrophages WITHOUT inflammation
Liquefaction into pus and neutrophil infiltration
Calcium soap saponification
questions.explanation: Apoptotic cells fragment into membrane-wrapped bodies exposing 'eat-me' signals (phosphatidylserine), ensuring prompt macrophage clearance without tissue inflammation.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 9 & Slide 12 — Apoptosis Morphology: • Cell shrinks -> Chromatin condenses -> Membrane starts blebbing -> Apoptotic bodies form -> Macrophages phagocytose -> NO inflammation.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is Dystrophic Calcification, and what are typical serum calcium levels in patients presenting with it?
options: Calcium deposition in normal tissues secondary to hypercalcemia; serum calcium is elevated
Calcium deposition in dead, damaged, or necrotic tissues; serum calcium levels are NORMAL
Calcium deposition in healthy bone; serum calcium is decreased
Calcium loss from the skeleton; serum calcium is zero
questions.explanation: Local damaged matrix vesicles bind calcium phosphate regardless of normal circulating serum calcium levels.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 25 — Dystrophic Calcification: • Dystrophic Calcification: Calcium deposits in dead or damaged tissue | Serum calcium levels normal | Seen in areas of necrosis, atherosclerotic plaques, damaged heart valves, and TB caseous foci.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is Metastatic Calcification, and what is its primary underlying systemic cause?
options: Calcium deposition in normal healthy tissues secondary to HYPERCALCEMIA (e.g., hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D toxicity, renal failure)
Calcium deposition in necrotic heart valves with normal serum calcium
Spread of bone cancer to visceral organs
Calcium loss from kidneys
questions.explanation: Systemic hypercalcemia supersaturates interstitial fluids, driving calcium salt precipitation in healthy organs (interstitium of kidney, lung, gastric mucosa).
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 25 — Metastatic Calcification: • Metastatic Calcification: Calcium deposits in otherwise normal tissue | Secondary to hypercalcemia (hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D toxicity, renal failure).

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Which organs are classically and preferentially affected by Metastatic Calcification due to their alkaline internal compartments?
options: Interstitium of the kidney, lung, and gastric mucosa
Skeletal muscle and myocardium
Central nervous system and spinal cord
Spleen and lymph nodes
questions.explanation: These tissues secrete acid, creating an internal alkaline local environment that favors calcium salt precipitation when serum calcium is elevated.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 25 — Metastatic Calcification Favorite Sites: • Favors interstitium of kidney, lung, and gastric mucosa.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What are the four major categories of Intracellular Accumulations discussed in the pathology lecture?
options: Lipids (Steatosis), Glycogen, Proteins, and Pigments
Water, Sodium, Potassium, and Chloride
DNA, RNA, Histones, and Enzymes
Fibrin, Collagen, Elastin, and Reticulin
questions.explanation: Metabolic overproduction, abnormal storage, or defective degradation leads to intracellular accumulation of these four substance classes.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 23 — Intracellular Accumulations: • Intracellular Accumulations: Lipids (Steatosis) | Glycogen | Proteins | Pigments.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What causes intracellular accumulation of Glycogen, and in which conditions is it classically seen?
options: Abnormal glucose metabolism, such as Diabetes Mellitus and Glycogen Storage Diseases
Starvation and protein deficiency
Iron overload and thalassemia
Lipofuscin wear-and-tear pigment deposition
questions.explanation: Impaired glucose processing leads to excessive glycogen vacuolization in renal tubular epithelium, liver cells, and beta cells.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 23 — Glycogen Accumulation: • Glycogen: Abnormal glucose metabolism: Diabetes mellitus, glycogen storage diseases.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What are classic examples of abnormal intracellular Protein accumulations?
options: Mallory-Denk bodies (alcoholic liver disease) and alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency globules
Cholesterol clefts in atheroma
Calcium phosphate soap crystals
Hemosiderin iron granules
questions.explanation: Accumulation of misfolded structural proteins forms intracellular inclusion bodies like Mallory hyaline in alcoholic steatohepatitis.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 23 — Protein Accumulation: • Proteins: Misfolded / excess proteins: e.g., Mallory-Denk bodies, a1-antitrypsin deficiency.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What are the four major Pigments that accumulate intracellularly?
options: Lipofuscin ('wear-and-tear' pigment), Melanin, Hemosiderin (iron overload), and Bilirubin
Hemoglobin, Myoglobin, Fibrin, and Albumin
Keratin, Collagen, Elastin, and Mucin
Glucose, Cholesterol, Triglyceride, and Lactate
questions.explanation: Endogenous pigments accumulate within cells due to normal aging wear-and-tear, chronic hemorrhage, or metabolic pigment synthesis disorders.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 23 — Pigments: • Pigments: Lipofuscin ('wear-and-tear'), melanin, hemosiderin (iron overload).

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is Lipofuscin, and why is it frequently referred to as the 'wear-and-tear' pigment?
options: An exogenous carbon tattoo pigment
An insoluble golden-brown intracellular pigment composed of polymers of lipid and phospholipid complexes derived from free radical lipid peroxidation, accumulating steadily with age
An iron storage complex found in hemochromatosis
A pathological calcium salt deposit
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin represents undigested lipid peroxidation residues accumulating in long-lived postmitotic cells (heart, liver, brain) with advancing age.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 23 — Lipofuscin: • Lipofuscin ('wear-and-tear pigment').

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is the key difference between Necrosis and Apoptosis regarding cell size, membrane integrity, and inflammation?
options: Necrosis: Cell swelling, disrupted leaky membrane, inflammation present; Apoptosis: Cell shrinkage, intact membrane (apoptotic bodies), no inflammation
Necrosis: Cell shrinkage without inflammation; Apoptosis: Cell swelling with massive pus
Both forms of cell death cause identical inflammatory responses
Neither form involves membrane changes
questions.explanation: This contrast summarizes why necrosis provokes collateral tissue damage and inflammation whereas apoptosis is immunologically silent.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 14 — Necrosis vs. Apoptosis Table: • Necrosis: Cell size = Swelling | Plasma membrane = Disrupted, leaky | Inflammation = Yes | Apoptosis: Cell size = Shrinkage | Plasma membrane = Intact, blebs | Inflammation = No.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is the energy requirement difference between Necrosis and Apoptosis?
options: Necrosis requires active ATP generation; Apoptosis is energy-independent
Necrosis is independent (passive, accidental); Apoptosis is active and energy-dependent (ATP-requiring)
Both require massive ATP consumption
Neither requires energy
questions.explanation: Apoptosis requires ATP to run caspase activation cascades and apoptotic body formation, whereas necrosis occurs when ATP is completely depleted.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 14 — Necrosis vs. Apoptosis Table: • Energy requirement: Necrosis = Independent (passive) | Apoptosis = Dependent — active, ATP-requiring.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is the final tissue outcome following Necrosis versus Apoptosis?
options: Necrosis: Often replaced by fibrous scar tissue; Apoptosis: Bodies phagocytosed by macrophages with no scar
Necrosis: Resolves completely with zero scarring; Apoptosis: Always forms a large fibrotic scar
Both always result in organ calcification
Neither has any tissue outcome
questions.explanation: Because necrosis destroys stroma and recruits inflammatory cells, tissue repair frequently results in scarring; apoptosis maintains normal architecture.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 14 — Necrosis vs. Apoptosis Table: • Tissue outcome: Necrosis = Often replaced by scar | Apoptosis = Bodies phagocytosed; no scar.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: In which clinical condition is Dystrophic Calcification commonly found by surgeons?
options: Healthy normal skin
Atherosclerotic plaques, damaged heart valves, areas of old necrosis, and TB caseous granulomas
Blood serum of normal healthy young adults
Normal skeletal muscle tissue
questions.explanation: Degenerating lipid-rich or necrotic tissue readily binds circulating calcium, creating clinically significant calcific aortic stenosis or atheroma plaques.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 25 — Dystrophic Calcification: • Seen in areas of necrosis, atherosclerotic plaques, damaged heart valves, and TB caseous foci.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What triggers the accumulation of Hemosiderin inside cells?
options: Local or systemic iron overload (e.g., chronic hemorrhage, bruising, or hemochromatosis), where excess iron is polymerized into golden-brown ferritin-derived micelles
Severe protein deficiency
Acute dehydration
Excess carbohydrate intake
questions.explanation: Excess intracellular iron is sequestered into golden-brown hemosiderin granules visible in macrophages within old hematomas or iron overload states.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 23 — Pigments (Hemosiderin): • Hemosiderin (iron overload).

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is Cellular Aging, and what are its primary molecular drivers?
options: Progressive accumulation of cellular and molecular damage over time leading to decreased functional capacity, driven by DNA damage accumulation, telomere shortening, defective protein homeostasis, and mitochondrial dysfunction
Acute bacterial infection acquired in the operating theatre
Rapid cellular regeneration in response to hormones
Reversible hydropic swelling of hepatocytes
questions.explanation: Aging reflects the cumulative breakdown of cellular maintenance mechanisms and replicative exhaustion.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 15 — Cellular Aging: • Cellular Aging: Progressive accumulation of cellular and molecular damage over time, leading to decreased functional capacity and viability | DNA damage accumulation outpacing repair | Telomere shortening -> replicative senescence | Defective protein homeostasis | Deregulated nutrient sensing & mitochondrial dysfunction.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is the specific surgical relevance of Cellular Aging in elderly patients undergoing major operations?
options: Impaired wound healing and reduced physiologic reserve increase perioperative and anesthetic risk
Elderly patients have identical physiological reserve to neonates
Wound healing is accelerated in elderly patients
Aging has zero impact on surgical outcomes
questions.explanation: Decreased tissue perfusion, diminished organ functional reserve, and delayed fibroplasia elevate postoperative complication rates in geriatric surgery.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 15 — Cellular Aging Surgical Relevance: • Surgical relevance: impaired wound healing and reduced physiologic reserve increase perioperative and anesthetic risk in elderly patients.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: How does the Stress Response Spectrum describe the fate of a normal cell exposed to injurious stimuli?
options: Normal homeostasis → Adaptation → Reversible Injury (stimulus removed, recovery possible) → Irreversible Injury (necrosis or apoptosis cell death)
Normal homeostasis → Immediate death without adaptation
Adaptation → Direct conversion to malignancy
Reversible injury always leads to cancer
questions.explanation: Cells mount an orderly hierarchy of defense, adapting to mild stress or recovering from reversible injury before crossing the threshold to death.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 5 — The Stress Response Spectrum: • Normal Cell Homeostasis maintained -> Adaptation -> Reversible Injury (stimulus removed, recovery possible) -> Irreversible Injury (necrosis or apoptosis cell death).

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What factors determine whether an injured cell adapts, recovers, or dies?
options: The type, duration, and severity of the injury, as well as the cell's own adaptability, metabolic state, and blood supply
The operating room temperature and humidity
The surgeon's preference
The hospital's billing code
questions.explanation: Vulnerable myocardial cells infarct rapidly under ischemia, whereas robust fibroblasts tolerate transient hypoxia much better.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 5 — Stress Response Determinants: • Whether a cell adapts, recovers, or dies depends on the type, duration, and severity of the injury, as well as the cell's own adaptability, metabolic state, and blood supply.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is the primary role of intraoperative frozen-section pathology in guiding surgical oncology?
options: Assessing surgical resection margins and regional lymph node status to ensure complete tumor removal
Calculating hospital billing charges
Administering general anesthesia
Closing skin incisions
questions.explanation: Intraoperative frozen section examination of margins prevents leaving positive cancer behind during tumor extirpation.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 18 — Intraoperative Pathology: • Intraoperative Pathology: Recognizing necrosis patterns aids frozen-section margin assessment.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Why is understanding Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury critical during vascular clamp release or organ transplantation?
options: Because restoring blood flow generates a massive oxidative burst of ROS and inflammation that can damage the newly reperfused organ or cause systemic reperfusion syndrome
Because blood flow restoration has zero physiological impact
Because clamps prevent all cell death
Because reperfusion cools the organ
questions.explanation: Releasing vascular cross-clamps floods ischemic tissue with oxygen radicals, initiating complement activation and endothelial cell damage.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 3 & Slide 18 — Ischemia-Reperfusion: • Ischemia reperfusion injury is central to many surgical scenarios — transplant, vascular, and reconstructive.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: How does the management of dry gangrene differ fundamentally from wet gangrene in surgical practice?
options: Dry gangrene involves mummification without infection and can often be managed expectantly or allowed to auto-amputate, whereas wet gangrene is a surgical emergency requiring immediate debridement/amputation to prevent fatal sepsis
Both conditions require identical emergency amputation within 1 hour
Neither condition requires any medical or surgical attention
Wet gangrene is managed solely with warm saline
questions.explanation: Septic bacterial proliferation in wet/gas gangrene drives fatal bacteremia, whereas dry gangrene remains localized and sterile.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 21 & Slide 22 — Gangrene Management: • Gangrene Management: Dry vs. wet gangrene determines urgency, antibiotic need, and amputation level | Wet gangrene carries high risk of sepsis and demands urgent surgical intervention unlike dry gangrene which can sometimes be managed expectantly.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What histological and morphological features distinguish Apoptosis from Necrosis on H&E tissue examination?
options: Apoptosis shows single cell shrinkage, condensed chromatin, and apoptotic bodies without inflammation; Necrosis shows groups of swollen cells, membrane rupture, nuclear pyknosis/karyolysis, and acute inflammation
Apoptosis shows massive pus and neutrophil infiltration
Necrosis shows single cell shrinkage without inflammation
Both appear identical under the microscope
questions.explanation: Single-cell programmed deletion characterizes apoptosis, whereas confluent cell death with acute inflammation marks necrosis.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 9, Slide 12 & Slide 14 — Necrosis vs Apoptosis: • Apoptosis: Single cells, shrinkage, condensed chromatin, apoptotic bodies, no inflammation | Necrosis: Groups of cells, swelling, membrane disruption, pyknosis/karyolysis/karyorrhexis, acute inflammation.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is the role of Caspase-8 in the apoptotic cascade?
options: It is the initiator caspase activated by the extrinsic (death receptor) pathway
It is a mitochondrial enzyme that synthesizes ATP
It causes coagulative necrosis in the heart
It digests bacteria in pus
questions.explanation: Receptor clustering recruits FADD and procaspase-8, auto-catalytically activating caspase-8 to drive the executioner phase.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 12 — Extrinsic Pathway: • Extrinsic Pathway: Caspases-8 activation through receptor-mediated signaling.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What is the role of Cytochrome c release in the apoptotic cascade?
options: It leaks from damaged mitochondria into the cytosol during the intrinsic pathway to activate caspase-9 via the apoptosome
It causes tissue calcification
It binds calcium to form soap deposits
It synthesizes glycogen in the liver
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization releases cytochrome c into the cytoplasm, initiating intrinsic programmed cell death.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 11 & Slide 12 — Intrinsic Pathway: • Intrinsic Pathway: Cytochrome c release -> caspase-9 activation.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Why do intracellular accumulations of lipids (steatosis) occur predominantly in the liver?
options: Because the liver is the primary metabolic organ handling fat processing, lipoprotein synthesis, and triglyceride metabolism
Because the liver lacks blood vessels
Because the liver is composed entirely of adipose tissue
Because hepatocytes do not require ATP
questions.explanation: Alcohol toxicity, hypoxia, or malnutrition disrupts hepatic lipid export pathways, trapping triglycerides inside hepatocytes.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 7 & Slide 23 — Steatosis: • Fatty Change (Steatosis): Hypoxic, toxic, or metabolic injury - especially in the liver.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What pathological process underlies the formation of atherosclerotic plaques and damaged heart valve calcification?
options: Metastatic calcification due to hypercalcemia
Dystrophic calcification occurring in areas of previous tissue degeneration, necrosis, and lipid deposition with normal serum calcium
Glycogen storage disease
Apoptosis of endothelial cells
questions.explanation: Subendothelial lipid pools and necrotic core debris in atheromas undergo dystrophic calcium phosphate deposition over time.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 25 — Dystrophic Calcification: • Dystrophic Calcification: Calcium deposits in dead or damaged tissue | Serum calcium levels normal | Seen in areas of necrosis, atherosclerotic plaques, damaged heart valves.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: What clinical consequence arises from failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump during early reversible ischemic cell injury?
options: Intracellular accumulation of sodium and water, leading to acute hydropic cellular swelling
Massive extracellular calcium precipitation
Increased ATP synthesis
Accelerated protein transcription
questions.explanation: Loss of active ionic pumping collapses osmotic balance, swelling the cell body and cytoplasmic organelles.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 4 & Slide 16 — Hydropic Swelling & ATP: • Failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump -> Na+ and water enter the cell -> cellular swelling.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: Which form of cell death is always pathological, uncontrolled, and associated with acute inflammation?
options: Apoptosis
Necrosis
Physiological cell turnover
Embryogenic web regression
questions.explanation: Accidental necrotic cell destruction invariably liberates damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that incite acute inflammation.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 6 — Necrosis General Features: • Necrosis: Uncontrolled, energy-independent cell death occurring in living tissue. Triggers an inflammatory response and is always pathologic.

questions.subject: PATH2
questions.stem: According to the final summary of the lecture, what is the ultimate practical goal of understanding cell injury and death in surgery?
options: Recognizing patterns of cell death and injury thresholds directly guides surgical decision-making, debridement extent, organ preservation, and clinical prognosis
Passing medical terminology tests without clinical application
Writing pathology billing receipts
Avoiding all surgical operations in elderly patients
questions.explanation: Mastery of cellular pathology bridges basic science and operative judgment, directly optimizing patient outcomes in the OR.
questions.source: Cell Injury and Death — Lecture 2, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 1 & Slide 18 — Summary & Surgical Relevance: • Recognizing patterns of cell death directly guides surgical decision-making and prognosis | Cell injury is reversible until critical thresholds in ATP, calcium, and membrane integrity are crossed.
